subtype: Turning away as boundary or snub [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Elizabeth, and I still remember the day Anjali turned her back on me. I'd walked over at lunch with my tray, and she saw me, then swung round to face the wall. My stomach dropped. All afternoon I replayed it: what did I say, what did I do? I decided she was fed up with me and sat alone. By the last bell I was tired of guessing, so I caught her at the gate and asked, "Was everything okay at lunch?" She groaned. "Oh no. I was copying the maths homework before Sir collected it, I didn't even see your face." I felt silly, but also relieved I'd asked.

qa.q: What did Anjali do when Elizabeth walked over with a lunch tray?
qa.a: She swung round to face the wall.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth think Anjali's turning away meant, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Elizabeth took it as a snub and decided Anjali was fed up. The dropping stomach and sitting alone show Elizabeth felt hurt, though the real reason was homework.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth do next time someone turns away?
qa.a: Elizabeth could wait a little, not take it personally, and ask later, as happened at the gate. A calm question clears up guesswork.

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt when she heard Elizabeth's question?
qa.a: Anjali may have felt sorry and a little shocked that her hurry looked like a snub. She groaned and explained at once because she hadn't seen Elizabeth's face.

grounding: A teenager reads a peer turning away as a snub, but it was distraction, and asking later steadied the friendship.

subtype: Turning away as boundary or snub [Interpreting]
passage: Observation note, Ms. Leela, Class 9B. During free period Seema walked up to a classmate who was standing with her back partly turned. The classmate shifted further away without a word. Seema stopped, went red, and returned to her seat with her bag held tight against her chest. She told a friend, "She's ignoring me on purpose." I did not step in at that moment. At the end of the day I asked Seema to wait, and we talked. I suggested that turning away can mean many things, including being distracted, and that asking gently later might tell her more. She agreed to try tomorrow. I will check in.

qa.q: Which class does Ms. Leela's note describe?
qa.a: The note describes Class 9B.

qa.q: What was Seema likely feeling when she walked back to her seat, and what suggests it?
qa.a: She likely felt hurt and rejected, since she went red and held her bag tight against her chest. She told a friend the classmate was ignoring her on purpose, but this is her reading, not proof.

qa.q: What could Seema try tomorrow?
qa.a: She could ask the classmate gently, without accusing, whether it was a bad moment. That would show whether it was distraction or needing space.

qa.q: How might the classmate have seen the moment?
qa.a: They may have been distracted or wanted space and not noticed Seema's approach. If so, they had no idea the shift would feel like a snub.

grounding: A teenager reads a classmate's turning away as a snub, and a teacher points to other meanings and asking later.

subtype: Turning away as boundary or snub [Interpreting]
passage:
Tuesday
Today in the corridor I waved at Farhan and called his name. He looked at me for one second and then turned his whole body away and walked off toward the lab.
I stood there with my hand still up like an idiot. Two people saw.
All through maths I kept thinking, what did I do? Was it the joke about his bowling on Sunday? I decided I wouldn't talk to him either.
But at the bus stop he came up to me. "Sorry about this morning. Coach had just shouted at me in front of the whole team. I couldn't talk to anyone."
So it wasn't me at all. I'm glad I didn't send the angry message I typed at lunch.
- Mohit

qa.q: Where did Farhan walk off toward?
qa.a: Toward the lab.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling after Farhan turned away?
qa.a: Mohit felt snubbed and embarrassed, standing with a raised hand, and then worried that the bowling joke had upset Farhan.

qa.q: What went right in the end, and what could Mohit try next time?
qa.a: Not sending the angry message kept the friendship safe; next time Mohit could wait and ask later instead of deciding it was a snub.

qa.q: What was it like for Farhan when Mohit waved?
qa.a: Farhan had just been shouted at by the coach, so he likely felt upset and needed space, and turning away was about that, not about Mohit.

grounding: A teenager reads a friend turning away as a snub, but it was distress needing space, and asking later keeps the friendship steady.

subtype: Turning away as boundary or snub [Interpreting]
passage:
At the village bus stop, Alka saw Yogesh standing by the tea stall. She called out, "Yogesh! Coming to the fair?"
He glanced at her, then turned away, shoulders hunched, and stared at the road.
Alka's cheeks burned. They'd walked to school together for three years. What was that?
She was about to march over. But she noticed his father nearby, still speaking loudly to the tea seller about unpaid money, and Yogesh staring hard at the dust.
She stayed where she was.
In the evening, Yogesh came to her gate. "Sorry about the bus stop. Baba was shouting, and I didn't want anyone to talk to me right then."
"I thought you were ignoring me."
"Not you. Everyone."

qa.q: How many years had Alka and Yogesh walked to school together?
qa.a: Three years.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling when Yogesh turned away?
qa.a: Alka felt hurt and insulted, taking it as a snub from an old friend.

qa.q: What helped Alka avoid a needless fight?
qa.a: She noticed the context, his father shouting nearby, and chose not to confront Yogesh, waiting for him to explain.

qa.q: What was it like for Yogesh at the bus stop?
qa.a: Yogesh was probably embarrassed and wanted space, so turning away was about the scene with his father, not about Alka.

grounding: At a village bus stop, a teenager reads a friend turning away as a snub, but it was embarrassment and a need for space.

subtype: Turning away as boundary or snub [Interpreting]
passage: At the lockers of their Toronto high school, Camila spotted Bao and called, "Bao! Did you see the new art room?" Bao glanced at her, then turned his whole body towards the wall and pressed his forehead against his locker door. Camila's wave froze in the air. Great. What did I do? All through Spanish she replayed Friday: had she laughed too loudly at his drawing? She almost left him out of the plan for Saturday. Instead, after school, she found him on the bus bench and sat down a little distance away. "Hey. Earlier, did I do something?" Bao rubbed his eyes. "No. My grandma's in hospital. I'd just got a text. I couldn't talk to anyone." Camila nodded and simply sat with him until his bus came.

qa.q: What did Camila call out to Bao about?
qa.a: The new art room.

qa.q: What was Camila feeling when her wave froze in the air?
qa.a: Camila felt hurt and worried, sure she had done something wrong and replaying Friday to find it.

qa.q: What kept Camila's friendship with Bao steady?
qa.a: Not acting on the snub, such as leaving him out of Saturday's plan, and asking him quietly later instead.

qa.q: What was that moment at the lockers like for Bao?
qa.a: Bao had just learned his grandma was in hospital and was too upset to talk to anyone; turning away had nothing to do with Camila.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager reading a friend turning away as a snub when the friend needed space, and asking later instead of taking it personally.
